topic.subject: social
topic.title: The French Revolution
topic.scope: estates, storming of the Bastille, Declaration of Rights, Jacobins, Napoleon, ideas of liberty and equality

misconceptions.statement: The First and Second Estates also paid some taxes to the King.
misconceptions.why: Students assume that in any state, everyone must contribute some tax to the government.
misconceptions.fix: The First and Second Estates (Clergy and Nobility) were completely exempt from paying taxes to the state.

probe.question: Which estate was responsible for paying the 'taille' tax?
probe.wrong_answer: All three estates paid it, but the Third Estate paid more.

misconceptions.root_belief: rules of the present apply to the past

misconceptions.statement: The Bastille was full of hundreds of political prisoners when it was stormed.
misconceptions.why: The symbolic importance of the event leads students to exaggerate the scale of the rescue.
misconceptions.fix: There were only seven prisoners in the Bastille when it was stormed; it was attacked mainly for its gunpowder and as a symbol of tyranny.

probe.question: Why did the mob attack the Bastille?
probe.wrong_answer: To free the hundreds of innocent people the King had locked up.

misconceptions.root_belief: important events must have large-scale immediate results
misconceptions.source_hint: historical empathy studies in history education

misconceptions.statement: In the Estates General, every individual person had one vote.
misconceptions.why: Students project modern democratic voting norms onto historical assemblies.
misconceptions.fix: In the Estates General, each of the three estates had only one collective vote, regardless of the number of representatives.

probe.question: How was voting conducted in the Estates General before the Third Estate protested?
probe.wrong_answer: Each representative cast an individual vote.

misconceptions.root_belief: voting always means one person one vote

misconceptions.statement: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen gave equal rights to women.
misconceptions.why: The word 'Man' is often interpreted in modern English as 'humanity', leading to confusion.
misconceptions.fix: The Declaration specifically applied to men; women were excluded from these political rights and remained 'passive citizens'.

probe.question: Did the 1791 Constitution allow women to vote?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the Declaration said all citizens are equal.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: The Jacobins were a group of wealthy nobles who wanted to change the law.
misconceptions.why: Students often confuse different political factions or assume only the elite can lead a movement.
misconceptions.fix: The Jacobins mainly belonged to the less prosperous sections of society, like small shopkeepers, artisans, and daily-wage workers.

probe.question: Which social group formed the main base of the Jacobin club?
probe.wrong_answer: The wealthy aristocracy and high clergy.

misconceptions.root_belief: only the powerful can cause change

misconceptions.statement: The Reign of Terror was a period of lawless rioting by the poor.
misconceptions.why: Students associate 'terror' with chaotic street violence rather than state-sponsored policy.
misconceptions.fix: The Reign of Terror was a period of systematic state control and legal executions led by Robespierre's government.

probe.question: Who directed the executions during the Reign of Terror?
probe.wrong_answer: Angry mobs in the streets acting without any government.

misconceptions.root_belief: violence is always chaotic and unplanned

misconceptions.statement: Napoleon was a democratic leader because he overthrew the monarchy.
misconceptions.why: Students use binary logic: if he is against the old King, he must be for democracy.
misconceptions.fix: Napoleon was a military dictator who crowned himself Emperor of France in 1804, ending the Republic.

probe.question: What title did Napoleon take in 1804?

misconceptions.root_belief: the enemy of a tyrant is a democrat

misconceptions.statement: French women won the right to vote immediately after the Revolution ended.
misconceptions.why: Students assume that a revolution for 'liberty' must have achieved its goals for everyone quickly.
misconceptions.fix: Women in France did not get the right to vote until 1944, long after the French Revolution.

probe.question: When did women in France finally get the right to vote?
probe.wrong_answer: In 1789, right after the Bastille fell.

misconceptions.statement: Tithes were a tax paid by the Third Estate to the King.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the different types of taxes mentioned in the text.
misconceptions.fix: Tithes were a tax levied by the Church, comprising one-tenth of the agricultural produce.
misconceptions.root_belief: all taxes go to the government

misconceptions.statement: Slavery was permanently abolished in French colonies in 1794.
misconceptions.why: Students miss the fact that Napoleon reintroduced it later.
misconceptions.fix: While the Convention abolished slavery in 1794, Napoleon Bonaparte reintroduced it ten years later.

probe.question: What happened to slavery under Napoleon's rule?
probe.wrong_answer: It remained abolished as per the Revolutionary laws.

misconceptions.root_belief: history is a linear path of improvement

misconceptions.statement: The subsistence crisis was caused only by the King's bad decisions.
misconceptions.why: Students tend to blame a single person (the villain) for complex economic phenomena.
misconceptions.fix: The crisis was caused by a combination of a rising population and bad harvests due to drought or hail, which led to food shortages.

probe.question: What was a natural cause of the subsistence crisis in France?
probe.wrong_answer: The King decided to hide all the grain in his palace.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Active citizens were those who participated in street protests.
misconceptions.why: Students use the literal meaning of 'active' (physical movement) rather than the legal definition.
misconceptions.fix: Active citizens were men over 25 who paid a certain amount of taxes, giving them the right to vote.

probe.question: What qualified a person as an 'active citizen' in 1791?
probe.wrong_answer: Being a member of a revolutionary mob or club.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
